clinicalPearls: Most infections are caused by Candida albicans, a commensal yeast that becomes symptomatic when the vaginal environment or host defences change
Typical features are intense vulval itching, soreness, and a thick, white, non-malodorous discharge often likened to cottage cheese, with vulval erythema and sometimes fissuring
The vaginal pH usually remains normal and acidic, which helps distinguish it from bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis
Predisposing factors include recent antibiotic use, pregnancy, diabetes, immunosuppression, and high oestrogen states
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by microscopy showing budding yeasts and pseudohyphae, and culture is useful in recurrent or treatment-resistant cases to identify non-albicans species
Uncomplicated disease responds well to topical or oral antifungal therapy, whereas recurrent disease often needs a longer induction and maintenance approach
Recurrent or resistant infection should prompt evaluation for diabetes, immunosuppression, and non-albicans species such as Candida glabrata, which are less responsive to standard azoles
It is not classed as a sexually transmitted infection, and routine treatment of asymptomatic male partners is not indicated
reference.pathophysiology: Candida species colonise the vagina asymptomatically in many women, kept in check by the resident lactobacillus-dominant flora and local immunity. Disturbance of this balance, for example by antibiotics, or increased glycogen availability from high oestrogen states and hyperglycaemia, allows the yeast to proliferate and transform into an invasive hyphal form. Adherence to and penetration of the vaginal epithelium triggers a brisk inflammatory response, producing the pruritus, erythema, and discharge characteristic of symptomatic infection.
additionalInvestigations: Vaginal pH measurement, typically normal in candidiasis
Saline and potassium hydroxide wet-mount microscopy for yeasts and pseudohyphae
Fungal culture in recurrent, severe, or treatment-resistant cases to speciate
Blood glucose or HbA1c testing where recurrent infection suggests diabetes
Consideration of HIV or immunosuppression assessment in refractory disease
redFlags: Recurrent or refractory infection suggesting undiagnosed diabetes or immunosuppression
Severe vulval swelling, fissuring, or ulceration prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Systemic candidiasis in significantly immunocompromised patients
Failure to respond to standard azole therapy suggesting a non-albicans species
Coexisting symptoms pointing to another sexually transmitted infection
reference.prognosis: Uncomplicated vulvovaginal candidiasis responds rapidly to antifungal treatment with an excellent outlook. A minority of women develop recurrent disease that is troublesome and requires prolonged maintenance therapy, and outcomes in these cases improve when underlying predisposing factors and non-albicans species are identified and addressed.
pitfalls: Diagnosing thrush on symptoms alone and missing bacterial vaginosis or dermatoses
Repeatedly treating recurrent infection without investigating for diabetes or immunosuppression
Assuming all cases are Candida albicans and overlooking azole-resistant species
Attributing chronic vulval symptoms to candidiasis when a dermatological condition is responsible
management: Treat uncomplicated infection with a topical or single-dose oral azole antifungal such as clotrimazole or fluconazole
For recurrent disease, use an induction course followed by a maintenance suppressive azole regimen
For non-albicans or azole-resistant species, switch to an alternative agent such as intravaginal boric acid or nystatin guided by culture
Address predisposing factors by optimising glycaemic control, reviewing antibiotic use and managing immunosuppression
In pregnancy, use topical azoles and avoid oral fluconazole
Provide symptomatic vulval care with a bland emollient and treat associated vulvitis
Investigate recurrent or refractory disease for underlying diabetes or immunosuppression including HIV, with patient education on trigger avoidance
